workbooktitle: Recursion with the monks of Mons Komputarius
narr-arrival: *After a long journey the traveller reaches the temple of Mons Komputarius.*
narr-help: *The traveller asks for help. Each time the master answers only briefly and stays silent for a long while in between.*
narr-tray: *The traveller puts his cards on a tray and carries it to the master.*
narr-select-a: *The largest card is taken from the tray and held back each time: first the **9**, then the **7**.*
narr-select-b: *Then come the **4** and finally the **2**. Every card held back waits for the way back.*
narr-empty: *The tray is now empty and is passed on to the waiting monks.*
narr-insert-a: *On the way back each held card is inserted on the left, the smaller ones move to the right: first the **2**, then the **4**.*
narr-insert-b: *Then the **7** and the **9**. The row now reads from left to right: **9, 7, 4, 2**.*
narr-sorted: *The sorted tray is handed to the traveller.*
narr-count-red: *The traveller takes the top (red) brick off the tower, puts it aside and makes a tally mark on the paper.*
narr-count-yellow: *Then the yellow brick: take it off, put it aside, second tally mark.*
narr-count-blue: *Finally the blue brick. The tower is gone, and three tally marks are on the paper.*
narr-count-rebuild: *The traveller takes the brick he put aside last and puts it back on the floor. On top of it he puts the brick he put aside before that, and so on, until the tower stands exactly as before.*
introduction:
A traveller is looking for a solution for his unsorted cards. The monks show him a way in which a problem keeps getting smaller and the solution is built on the way back.

Use the **Back** and **Next** buttons to go through the story.
functionalexplanation: A function’s implementation is called **functional** if it has no mutable state stored outside the function, such as a tally sheet.
warningdialogue: **Head monk:** “That does not surprise me … anyone who rushes into action so quickly will inevitably run past every solution.”
cards-demanddialogue: **Traveller:** “My cards! They need to be sorted!”
journey-questiondialogue: **Head monk:** “My dear stranger … how long did you travel to get here?”
return-questiondialogue: **Head monk:** “And how long will your return journey take?”
patiencedialogue: **Head monk:** “My dear stranger … I can show you our ways. But whether you will understand them … that I cannot promise. They are not difficult … but they require a calmness you seem to lack …”
tray-instructiondialogue: **Head monk:** “Put the cards on the tray.”
emptydialogue: **Head monk:** “My dear stranger … you seek solutions, yet you fail to see a solution even when it is right in front of you …”
givebackdialogue: **Head monk:** “Stranger … give him back the tray!”
sorteddialogue: **Head monk:** “My dear stranger. You now know our ways. Go out and use our knowledge whenever you need it. And do not worry: it does not take a temple full of monks to complete the task. Discipline and calm are quite enough!”
understooddialogue: **Traveller:** “I understand completely! I know I can do this on my own. I may not have enough hands … but there is plenty of room on my table. Thank you, great master!”
farewelldialogue: **Head monk:** “I see you have understood. Go now … and approach things a little more calmly in future!”
family-child-questiondialogue: **Child:** “Do you know how big it is?”
count-explanationdialogue: **Traveller:** “No, sweetheart … but I know how we can find out!”
count-grandmadialogue: **Grandma:** “The monks wouldn't have needed a piece of paper for this.”
kochtitle: Programming recursion yourself: the Koch curve
kochintroduction:
Now you will program your own recursive algorithm. The **Koch curve** is created by replacing each line segment with four shorter segments: the middle third becomes a triangular peak. The distance from start to finish remains **270 steps**.

Open the editor. You can work in **Java** or with your own **Snap! blocks**. Use a function with the parameters **length** and **depth**, and carry it over from one exercise to the next. The preview shows the target drawing and your result. The red arrows in the template indicate directions; they are not part of the drawing.
koch0: Draw a horizontal line **270 steps** to the right. Write a function `koch(length, depth)`. When `depth == 0`, it draws a segment with `forward(length)` and finishes. First call it with length **270** and depth **0**. This is the **base case** of your recursive function.
koch1: Extend the same function: for a greater depth, divide the length by **3** and call `koch` **four times** with the shorter length and a depth reduced by **1**. Between calls, turn **60° left**, **120° right** and **60° left**. Draw the target curve with length **270** and depth **1**. Each of its four segments is **90 steps** long. The turtle faces right again at the end. Use recursive calls rather than four hard-coded `forward` commands.
koch2: Reuse your function from task 4.2. Change only the depth of the initial call to **2**. Each of the four segments is now replaced by the same pattern again: this produces **16 segments**, each **30 steps** long. Compare your drawing with the target. Check whether you can use the same function for depths **0**, **1** and **2**. As you trace execution, ask yourself: what is simplified, when does a call end, and how do the four partial drawings form the next curve?
partzero: Getting to know the Eva editor
partdintro:
Now you draw recursively with the building bricks from part 2. The methods you wrote there are already available in every editor of this part:

- `stein(breite)` draws a building brick of width `breite` and height 20. Afterwards the turtle is back at the starting point, facing right.
- `hoch()` and `runter()` move the turtle up or down by one brick height (20) without drawing.
- `springe(weite)` moves the turtle forward by `weite` without drawing; with a negative distance it moves backwards.

Apart from these methods you only need `Turtle.forward`, `Turtle.turnLeft` and `Turtle.turnRight`.
cat-state: Keep track of the intermediate result
zerointro:
**How the Eva editor works:** Open it with **Open Editor** next to a task. At the top you choose whether you program with **Snap!** blocks or in **Java** (cup icon). When you switch, your program is translated into the other language. In the Java editor the methods of your class are listed on the left: clicking a method opens only that method, **Full source** shows the whole code. On the right under **Drawing** you start your program with **Run**. There you see the target drawing and your drawing on top of each other and find out whether they match. Your code is saved automatically. Close the editor with the cross at the top right.

In the tasks you draw with a **turtle** that initially faces right. It understands five commands:

- `Turtle.forward(x)`: move x steps forward
- `Turtle.turnLeft(w)` and `Turtle.turnRight(w)`: turn w degrees to the left or right
- `Turtle.penUp()` and `Turtle.penDown()`: lift or lower the pen

You write your code in a class with a `main` method, and your own methods as `static void`.

In this part you also write the methods `stein` (brick), `hoch` (up), `runter` (down) and `springe` (jump). In part 3 you use them to draw towers and pyramids of building bricks.
e1prompt: The turtle should draw a **building brick**: a rectangle, 60 wide and 20 high.
e2prompt:
1. Write a method `stein(breite)` that draws a building brick of the given width and height 20. Afterwards, the turtle must be back at the starting point, facing right.
2. Write a method `hoch()` that moves the turtle up by 20 **without drawing**, and a method `runter()` that moves it down by 20 in the same way. It keeps facing right in both cases.
3. Use them to draw three stacked bricks of widths 80, 60 and 40 (starting at the bottom, all left-aligned).

You do not need `runter()` here yet, but you will in part 3.
e3prompt:
Write a method `vieleck(ecken, laenge)` that draws a regular polygon. Use a loop.

Also write a method `springe(weite)` that moves the turtle `weite` steps forward **without drawing**; with a negative distance it moves backwards. Use it to draw a square (side length 60), jump 100 to the right and draw a hexagon (side length 40) there.

*Hint:* after a full round, the turtle has turned by 360° in total.
schemaintro: All recursive solutions of the monks follow the same scheme. Note: the simplification produces **two** things, the separated part and the rest.
a1prompt: Put the events in the correct order.
a1-item0: The traveller puts his cards on the tray.
a1-item1: The head monk takes the card with the highest value and has the tray passed on.
a1-item2: Every further monk takes the largest remaining card.
a1-item3: The last monk takes the last card.
a1-item4: The traveller receives the empty tray and returns it.
a1-item5: The last monk puts his card on the tray.
a1-item6: Every monk before him pushes the cards to the right and adds his card on the left.
a1-item7: The head monk adds his card on the left and pushes the cards together.
a2-caption: The traveller arrives with the cards **7 2 9 4 5**. The head monk is the 1st monk.
a2-row0: a) How many cards are on the tray when it reaches the 3rd monk?
a2-row1: b) Which card does the 3rd monk take?
a2-row2: c) Which cards are on the tray from left to right right after the 3rd monk has put down his card? (separated by spaces)
a2-row3: d) How many monks are needed for 5 cards?
a3-question: As in task 0.2, the traveller arrives with the cards 7 2 9 4 5. In which order are the cards on the tray at the end (from left to right)?
a4prompt: Assign each scene to the matching element. Elements may occur several times or not at all.
a4-row0: A monk takes the largest card from the tray.
a4-row1: A monk has the tray with the remaining cards passed on.
a4-row2: The traveller receives the empty tray and returns it unchanged.
a4-row3: A monk adds his card on the left of the returned tray.
a4-row4: The traveller puts his cards on the tray.
ac-intro:
Now you write the work of a monk as a Java method `sort`. The cards on the tray are a string, for example `"7294"`; each character is one card. Two helper methods already exist:

- `largestCard(cards)` returns the largest card.
- `without(cards, card)` returns the cards without that one card.

Choose the matching code for each of the four gaps.
ac-1-question: Gap 1: The traveller receives the empty tray and returns it unchanged. How do you recognise the empty tray?
ac-2-question: Gap 2: Which card does the monk take from the tray?
ac-3-question: Gap 3: How does the monk get the remaining cards back sorted?
ac-4-question: Gap 4: The monk adds his card on the left. What does he return?
a5prompt: Assign the parts of your method from task 0.5 to the elements of the scheme.
a6-question: Every monk holds a card in his hand while the others continue working. Which statements about this card are true?
a6-opt0: It is passed on to the next monk.
a6-opt1: It corresponds to the local variable `largest`.
a6-opt2: It is the return value of the call.
a6-opt3: It is kept while the further calls are running.
a6-opt4: It is a global variable that all monks access.
a6-opt5: It is not needed again until combining.
a7-question: What does the head monk need to know or be able to do to perform his task correctly?
a7-opt0: How many monks stand behind him.
a7-opt1: That he gets back a sorted tray with all remaining cards.
a7-opt2: Which card the last monk takes.
a7-opt3: How to combine his own card with the returned tray.
a7-opt4: How the other monks add their cards.
a7-opt5: What to do when the tray arrives empty.
a8intro: The traveller says: “I don't have enough hands … but there is enough room on my table.”
a8a-question: What corresponds to the traveller's table in the computer?
a8a-opt0: A loop that processes the cards one after another
a8a-opt1: The call stack, on which every call stores its local variables
a8a-opt2: A global list that all monks write into
a8a-opt3: The return value of the method
a8b-caption: The traveller sorts 5 cards on his own. How many calls of `sort` are active at the same time at most?
a8c-question: What happens if the traveller brings very, very many cards?
a8c-opt0: The method is automatically turned into a loop.
a8c-opt2: The table becomes too small: the program aborts with a `StackOverflowError`.
a8c-opt3: The cards are only partially sorted, without an error message.
c0prompt: Read the continuation of the play. The traveller is back home by now.
c1prompt: Assign each action of the traveller to the matching element.
c1-row0: He takes the top brick from the tower.
c1-row1: He makes a tally mark on the tally list.
c1-row2: He looks at the smaller tower and carries on in the same way.
c1-row3: Nothing is left of the tower; he counts the tally marks.
c1-row4: He puts the bricks from the table back together into the tower.
c2-caption: The child has a tower of 3 bricks. At the start the tally list is empty and nothing is on the table. State what it looks like **right before each recursive call**.
c2b-caption: How often is the method called in total (counting the first call)?
c3prompt: Here are three Java methods that count the bricks of a tower. A tower is a string, each character is a brick (e.g. `"RYB"`). `tower.substring(1)` is the tower without its top brick. Assign the matching variant to each description.
c3-row0: The traveller keeps the tally list on a piece of paper next to the table.
c3-row1: The paper with the tally list is passed on with the tower at every step.
c3-row2: The monks: each one puts a brick on the tray when handing it back.
c4-caption: Look at the methods from task 1.3 and state the values.
c4-row0: a) `countA("RYB");` is executed twice in a row. What value does `tally` have afterwards?
c4-row3: d) `countC("RYB")` is called twice in a row. What does the second call return?
c5-question: Which statements about the variants from task 1.3 are true?
c5-opt0: Variant B is not functional because an intermediate result is carried along.
c5-opt2: Functional recursion always needs a return path on which calculations are made.
c5-opt4: Variant A gives a wrong result on the second count if `tally` is not reset.
e4prompt:
In task 2.2 you stacked three bricks with separate calls. Now a **recursive** method takes over, just like the tower from the story. Write `zeichneTurm(n)` that draws a tower of `n` bricks of width 40. Do not use a loop.

- If the tower has no bricks, there is nothing to do.
- Otherwise: draw a brick, go up one brick height with `hoch()`, then draw the rest of the tower (one brick fewer).
e5prompt:
Write a recursive method `zeichnePyramide(n)`. The main program uses it to draw two pyramids next to each other. The second one only ends up in the right place if the turtle is back at its starting point after the first pyramid.

- For `n == 0` there is nothing to do.
- Otherwise: draw a brick of width `n * 20`. Then move to the next layer with `hoch()` and `springe(10)` and draw a pyramid with `n - 1` layers.
- **Afterwards**, bring the turtle back to where the call began with `springe(-10)` and `runter()`.
e6aprompt:
The program should draw the same two pyramids as in task 3.2, but it does not. Find the error and fix it.

In plain Java the program would abort with a `StackOverflowError`.
e6bprompt: The program should draw the same two pyramids as in task 3.2, but it does not. Find the error and fix it.
d1a-question: Where is the turtle right after the call `zeichnePyramide(3)` if the method works as described in task 3.2?
d1a-opt0: On the top layer of the pyramid
d1a-opt1: At the same point and facing the same direction as before the call
d1a-opt2: That depends on how large `n` is
d1a-opt3: To the right of the bottom layer
d1b-question: `zeichnePyramide(4)` calls `zeichnePyramide(3)`. What must the call with 4 be able to rely on?
d1b-opt0: That the turtle is at the very top after the call.
d1b-opt1: That a pyramid with 3 layers is drawn.
d1b-opt2: That the call with 3 also draws the bottom layer.
d1b-opt3: That the turtle is afterwards back where the call with 3 began.
d1b-opt4: That the call with 3 knows how wide the layer below it is.
d1note: As with the monks, every call has a **contract**: you only think about your own level and rely on the contract of the call.
e7prompt:
Write a recursive method `cantor(breite, n)` that draws a **Cantor wall**: one brick; below it, a brick of a third of the width only under its left and its right third; below those again under their left and right thirds, and so on.

- Draw a brick of width `breite`.
- If `n == 0`, you are done.
- Otherwise: leave a gap of one brick height with `runter()` twice and call `cantor` for the **left third** with a third of the width and `n - 1`.
- Then go right by two thirds of the width with `springe` and do the same for the **right third**.
- Finally, bring the turtle back to where the call began with `springe` and `hoch()` twice.
e7b-caption: How many bricks are drawn in total for `cantor(270, 3)`?
e8prompt:
Write a recursive method `baum(laenge, n)` that draws a tree. A tree consists of a trunk on which two smaller trees grow: one tilted to the left, one to the right.

- For `n == 0` there is nothing to do.
- Otherwise: draw the trunk (`laenge` forward).
- Turn 30° to the left and draw a tree with 60 % of the length and `n - 1`.
- Turn 60° to the right and draw another such tree.
- Turn the turtle back to the original direction and bring it back to the foot of the trunk with `springe(-laenge)`.
